Scarcely
skars'ly
adv. (hardly; with difficulty; barely)
From scarce, Old French escars, sparing, from Late Latin excarpsus. To do a thing scarcely is to do it barely, with difficulty, and nearly not at all.

Biblical Definition

Two occurrences, and both are arguments from difficulty. Paul measures the love of God by a human scale and finds the scale far too short: “For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die” (Rom 5:7). Men hardly ever die for the righteous; occasionally one might for a genuinely good man. And then the contrast: “But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom 5:8). Not for the righteous, not for the good, but for sinners — the one category no man dies for. Peter's use runs the other way, as a warning: “And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1Pe 4:18), quoting Proverbs 11:31. The scarcely there does not question the certainty of salvation; it describes its difficulty — what it cost, and the fire the saved pass through. Peter has just been writing about fiery trial. If the way home is that hard for those who are being saved, the position of those who are not is unspeakable.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines scarcely as hardly; with difficulty; and scarce as not plentiful; being in small quantity in proportion to the demand.

expand to see more

SC'ARCELY, adv.

1. Hardly; with difficulty.

Slowly he sails, and scarcely stems the tides.

We scarcely could persuade ourselves of the fact.

2. Hardly; scantily. Scarcely for a righteous man will one die. Rom. 5. From escars, sparing, niggardly.

Key Scripture

Romans 5:7 — "For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die."

Romans 5:8 — "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."

1 Peter 4:18 — "And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?"

Proverbs 11:31 — "Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner."

Modern Corruption

God's love is presented as a response to something lovable in man, which destroys the entire force of Paul's scarcely.

expand to see more

The most common misstatement of the gospel in our time is that God loves us because He sees our worth. Romans 5:7-8 was written to make that reading impossible. Paul sets up the best case human love can produce — a man might peradventure die for a genuinely good man — and then says God's love went where human love never goes: while we were yet sinners. If the object had been lovable, the demonstration would prove nothing. The word commendeth means God is exhibiting His love, putting it on display, and the display depends entirely on the unworthiness of those it fell upon. Self-worth preaching does not make this gospel warmer; it removes the thing that made it astonishing.

1 Peter 4:18 guards the opposite flank, against a cheapness that treats salvation as easy and therefore small. The righteous are scarcely saved — not doubtfully, for God keeps His own, but at enormous cost and through fire. Peter is writing to people under persecution and telling them the narrowness of the way is not a sign that something has gone wrong. The Reformed hold both without contradiction: salvation is certain because it rests on God's decree and Christ's finished work, and it is difficult because the road runs through a world at war with it. Certainty of arrival is not a promise of an easy passage.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek molis (G3433), with difficulty, hardly; sunistemi (G4921), to commend, to set together and display; Old French escars, sparing.

expand to see more

Greek molis (G3433) — with difficulty, scarcely; Romans 5:7, of dying for a righteous man.

Greek molis sozetai (G3433, G4982) — is scarcely saved; 1 Peter 4:18, of the righteous passing through fire.

Greek sunistesin (G4921) — He commends, exhibits, sets forth for display; Romans 5:8, God putting His love on show.

Greek hamartolon onton hemon (G268) — while we were sinners; the state, not the potential, that the love fell upon.

Old French escars — sparing, niggardly; Webster's root behind scarce.

Usage

"“Scarcely for a righteous man will one die” — the best human love can manage."

"“While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” — where human love never goes."

"“If the righteous scarcely be saved” — certain, and costly."
